1.topic: Overview of the Legislature under the Indian Constitution
1.lecture_title: Overview of the Legislature under the Indian Constitution: Parliament and State Legislatures
1.memory_hook: Think of the Indian Legislature as a massive two-storied democratic factory where the Lok Sabha represents the raw energy of the immediate masses, the Rajya Sabha acts as the cool-headed wise elder reviewing the blueprints, and the President is the final stamping authority who turns the bill into the law of the land.
1.concept_explanation:
At the heart of India's parliamentary democracy lies the Legislature, tasked with the supreme responsibility of law-making, representing public will, and holding the executive accountable. Established under Part V (Union Legislature) and Part VI (State Legislature) of the Constitution, the Indian legislative framework mirrors the Westminster model, yet is uniquely adapted to a federal structure with a unitary bias. The Union Parliament is not merely a bicameral body consisting of the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha; constitutionally, under Article 79, the Parliament comprises the Lok Sabha, the Rajya Sabha, and the President of India, emphasizing that no bill becomes law without executive assent.

The Lok Sabha (House of the People) is the directly elected chamber where members are chosen by universal adult suffrage representing territorial constituencies. It embodies the pulse of contemporary public opinion and holds the purse strings of the nation, particularly through Money Bills under Article 110. Conversely, the Rajya Sabha (Council of States) is a permanent, federal chamber representing the states and union territories. It insulates legislation from populist haste, ensuring that regional and minority interests are deliberated with sober reflection. While it cannot vote on demands for grants or initiate Money Bills, its concurrence is mandatory for ordinary legislation, and under Article 249, it possesses the extraordinary power to authorize Parliament to legislate on matters in the State List.

At the state level, the Legislature follows a similar bicameral or unicameral pattern under Article 168, consisting of the Governor and either one or two houses—the Legislative Assembly (Vidhan Sabha) and the Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad). While the Lok Sabha and Vidhan Sabha are dissolvable, the Rajya Sabha and Vidhan Parishad are continuous bodies where one-third of the members retire every two years. This structural architecture ensures stability, continuity, and democratic legitimacy, balancing popular sovereignty with constitutional checks and balances.
key_provisions: Article 79 — Constitution of Parliament consisting of the President and two Houses
Article 80 — Composition of the Council of States (Rajya Sabha)
Article 81 — Composition of the House of the People (Lok Sabha)
Article 168 — Constitution of Legislatures in States
Article 169 — Abolition or creation of Legislative Councils in States
Article 249 — Power of Parliament to legislate with respect to a matter in the State List in the national interest

case_laws.case_name: Ram Jawaya Kapur v. State of Punjab
case_laws.facts: The State of Punjab executed executive orders to monopolize the publishing and printing of school textbooks without enacting specific legislation. Private publishers challenged this, arguing that the executive government lacked the power to act without prior legislative sanction in a parliamentary democracy.
case_laws.holding: The Supreme Court held that the executive power of the State is co-extensive with its legislative power. The government can run businesses or execute policies even without prior legislation, provided it does not infringe upon fundamental rights or violate existing laws.
case_laws.why_it_matters: It establishes the foundational operational boundary between the legislature and the executive under the Indian constitutional scheme, clarifying that legislative sanction is only required when the executive infringes upon individual rights or requires taxation/spending authority.

case_laws.case_name: In re: Article 143, Constitution of India (Special Reference No. 1 of 1964) / Keshav Singh's Case
case_laws.facts: A conflict arose between the Uttar Pradesh Legislative Assembly and the High Court of Allahabad when the Assembly sentenced an individual for contempt of the House, and the High Court entertained a habeas corpus petition and granted bail. The Assembly viewed this judicial intervention as a breach of its legislative privileges.
case_laws.holding: The Supreme Court held that Indian legislatures do not possess absolute and unreviewable privileges akin to the British House of Commons. Fundamental rights, including personal liberty under Article 21, remain supreme, and courts have the jurisdiction to examine whether a legislative privilege has been validly exercised.
case_laws.why_it_matters: This landmark advisory opinion set the definitive boundaries of legislative privileges in India, ensuring that parliamentary sovereignty is subject to the written Constitution and judicial review.

1.real_world_example: When the Parliament passed the controversial three farm laws in 2020 without extensive select committee scrutiny, intense protests erupted across the nation. This contemporary event underscored the critical debate around legislative efficiency versus deliberative democracy, illustrating how the unicameral or fast-tracked passage of bills through voice votes without sending them to parliamentary committees can undermine the representative legitimacy of the legislature.
1.illustration: The State Legislature of Telangana passes a law regarding urban land ceilings. A group of citizens challenges the law, arguing that the Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad) did not vote on the bill within the constitutional time limit specified under Article 197. The constitutional question arises: can a bill become law if the upper house simply sits on it without a formal rejection or approval? Under Article 197, after a lapse of specified periods and re-passage by the Legislative Assembly, the bill is deemed passed by both houses, cementing the absolute legislative supremacy of the directly elected lower house.
1.quick_answer: The Indian Legislature functions at both Union and State levels, embodying a bicameral parliamentary system. Under Article 79, the Union Parliament consists of the President, the Lok Sabha, and the Rajya Sabha. The Lok Sabha represents the people directly through universal adult suffrage, holding ultimate control over national finances and the executive. The Rajya Sabha represents the states, functioning as a permanent federal reviewing chamber. At the state level, Article 168 provides for a Governor and either one or two houses (Vidhan Sabha and Vidhan Parishad). The legislature's core functions include law-making, financial control, and executive accountability. While parliamentary privileges grant immunity for internal proceedings, they are subject to judicial review to protect fundamental rights, as affirmed in Keshav Singh's case.
1.essay_answer:
Introduction: The Legislature is the cornerstone of India's democratic framework, responsible for translating the sovereign will of the people into binding legal norms. Operating under a parliamentary system of government, the Indian legislative architecture is dual-tiered, encompassing the Union Parliament (Part V) and State Legislatures (Part VI). It operates on the bedrock principles of representative democracy, federalism, and legislative supremacy within constitutional limits.

Composition of the Union Legislature: Article 79 establishes that the Parliament of India consists of the President and two Houses—the Council of States (Rajya Sabha) and the House of the People (Lok Sabha). The Lok Sabha (Article 81) is composed of members chosen by direct election from territorial constituencies. It is the popular chamber where governments are made or unmade through confidence motions. The Rajya Sabha (Article 80) consists of up to 250 members representing states and union territories, along with nominated members distinguished in literature, science, art, and social service. As a permanent house, it safeguards federal equilibrium.

State Legislatures: Under Article 168, states have a Legislature consisting of the Governor and either one House (Legislative Assembly or Vidhan Sabha) or two Houses (adding the Legislative Council or Vidhan Parishad). Article 169 empowers Parliament to create or abolish a Legislative Council upon a resolution passed by the State Assembly by a special majority. This reflects constitutional flexibility in accommodating state-specific administrative needs.

Powers, Functions, and Privileges: The primary function of the legislature is law-making across the Union, State, and Concurrent Lists under Schedule VII. Beyond legislation, it serves as the grand inquest of the nation, holding the executive accountable through question hour, zero hour, and motion debates. Additionally, legislative privileges (Articles 105 and 194) grant members freedom of speech within the house and immunity from legal proceedings for anything said during debates. However, as established in Keshav Singh's case, these privileges are not absolute and must harmonize with fundamental rights, subject to judicial scrutiny.

Conclusion: The Indian Legislature bridges the gap between state authority and citizen aspirations. Despite contemporary challenges like reduced debate hours and frequent disruptions, it remains the indispensable engine of constitutional governance, ensuring that power flows from the people through accountable representation.
1.exam_angle: Examiners frequently test this topic through direct essay questions on the composition and powers of Parliament or short notes on Legislative Privileges versus Fundamental Rights. To score top marks, avoid listing mere structural articles; instead, emphasize the federal dynamics of the Rajya Sabha and weave in landmark constitutional cases like Keshav Singh's case to demonstrate a mature understanding of institutional checks and balances.
quick_recap: Parliament = Lok Sabha + Rajya Sabha + President (Article 79).
Lok Sabha is directly elected and controls the purse strings.
Rajya Sabha is a permanent federal house protecting state interests.
State Legislatures can be unicameral or bicameral under Articles 168 and 169.
Legislative privileges under Articles 105 and 194 are subject to judicial review.
1.importance_reason: This topic forms the foundational bedrock of Unit I and sets up the entire institutional mechanics of the constitutional law paper, making it a guaranteed exam favorite for both short and essay questions.

2.topic: Composition and Structure of Union and State Legislatures
2.lecture_title: Composition and Structure of Union and State Legislatures: Articles 79 to 122 and 168 to 212
2.memory_hook: Think of India's Parliament as a grand royal court with a bicameral assembly: the Lok Sabha is the energetic House of the People representing heads, and the Rajya Sabha is the permanent Council of States representing regions, anchored by the President as the final royal seal.
2.concept_explanation:
Welcome to Unit I of Constitutional Law II. Today, we dissect the engine rooms of Indian democracy: the Union and State Legislatures. In a parliamentary democracy, the legislature is supreme in law-making, reflecting the collective will of over a billion citizens. Under the Indian Constitution, the Union Legislature, known as Parliament, consists of the President and two Houses: the Council of States (Rajya Sabha) and the House of the People (Lok Sabha). This bicameral structure is designed for checks and balances; while the Lok Sabha represents the direct mandate of the people through universal adult suffrage, the Rajya Sabha acts as a federal chamber, representing the states of the Union and bringing sober, deliberative wisdom to legislation.

At the state level, the architecture mirrors the Centre but with a crucial federal option: unicameralism versus bicameralism. Under Article 168, some states have a Legislative Assembly (Vidhan Sabha) alone, while others retain a Legislative Council (Vidhan Peshar/Vidhan Parishad) as an upper house. However, unlike the Rajya Sabha at the Centre which is a permanent federal necessity, a state Legislative Council is destructible and creatable under Article 169 through a resolution of the State Assembly and a law of Parliament. This dual structure ensures that local governance accommodates regional nuances while maintaining parliamentary supremacy.

The composition of these bodies is meticulously regulated by constitutional provisions and statutory frameworks like the Representation of the People Act, 1950 and 1951. Lok Sabha seats are allocated based on population to ensure territorial representation, while Rajya Sabha seats are distributed among states based on population schedules. Qualifications, disqualifications, disqualifications on grounds of defection under the Tenth Schedule, and the mechanics of anti-defection law all govern the behavior of members once inside these sacred halls. Understanding this architecture is essential because every law, tax, and constitutional amendment originates from the structural integrity of these legislative chambers.
key_provisions: Article 79 — Constitution of Parliament consisting of the President and two Houses.
Article 80 — Composition of the Council of States (Rajya Sabha).
Article 81 — Composition of the House of the People (Lok Sabha).
Article 168 — Constitution of Legislatures in States.
Article 169 — Abolition or creation of Legislative Councils in States.
Article 170 — Composition of the Legislative Assemblies in the States.
Article 171 — Composition of the Legislative Councils in the States.

case_laws.case_name: Ram Jawaya Kapur v. State of Punjab
case_laws.facts: The Punjab government issued executive notifications to run a printing and publishing business of school textbooks, which private publishers challenged, arguing the executive lacked legislative authorization to enter trade.
case_laws.holding: The Supreme Court held that the executive power of the State is co-extensive with its legislative power. The legislature does not need to pass an enabling act before the executive can embark on administrative functions, provided it does not infringe fundamental rights.
case_laws.why_it_matters: It establishes the foundational relationship between the executive and legislative arms, clarifying that executive action can run alongside legislative action as long as it does not violate statutory limits or fundamental rights.

case_laws.facts: Petitioners challenged the constitutional validity of the Tenth Schedule (Anti-Defection Law), arguing that vesting disqualification powers in the Speaker violated the basic structure doctrine and judicial review.
case_laws.holding: The Supreme Court upheld the Tenth Schedule and the sweeping powers of the Speaker, but struck down the portion that barred judicial review, holding that the Speaker acts as a tribunal whose decisions are subject to judicial review under Articles 136, 226, and 227.
case_laws.why_it_matters: It sets the boundaries for legislative discipline, defining the constitutional status of Speakers' decisions regarding floor-crossing and maintaining the supremacy of judicial review.

2.real_world_example: When the Parliament recently passed major criminal law overhauls (the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, etc.), debates erupted over bills being rushed through Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha with limited scrutiny from standing committees. This real-world friction highlights why the composition and procedural rules of our legislatures matter: when the opposition is sidelined or when upper houses are bypassed in urgency, the deliberative quality of Indian legislation faces severe democratic stress.
2.illustration: The State of Karnayana wants to abolish its Legislative Council because it feels the upper house is a redundant financial burden. The Legislative Assembly passes a resolution with a simple majority of members present and voting. However, the Parliament refuses to pass any law under Article 169 to abolish it. Can the State unilaterally dissolve its upper house? Step-by-step: Under Article 169, the State Assembly's resolution is only a recommendation; the final power to create or abolish a Legislative Council vests exclusively in Parliament through ordinary legislation. Therefore, Karnayana's Council remains intact.
2.quick_answer: The composition and structure of Union and State legislatures form the bedrock of India's parliamentary democracy. Parliament (Union Legislature) under Article 79 comprises the President, the Council of States (Rajya Sabha), and the House of the People (Lok Sabha). The Lok Sabha has a maximum strength of 550 elected members representing territorial constituencies, while the Rajya Sabha has a maximum of 250 members representing states and union territories, along with 12 nominated members. At the state level (Article 168), legislatures may be bicameral (Assembly and Council) or unicameral (Assembly only). State Legislative Assemblies (Vidhan Sabha) are directly elected based on adult suffrage under Article 170. State Legislative Councils (Vidhan Parishad), regulated by Article 171, can be created or abolished by Parliament upon a resolution passed by the State Assembly under Article 169. Together, these bodies exercise supreme law-making powers, subject to constitutional limitations and judicial review.
2.essay_answer:
Introduction

The structure of a legislature determines the health of a democracy. In India, the framers of the Constitution deliberately adopted a parliamentary system of governance, choosing a bicameral structure at the Union level and offering a flexible choice of unicameralism or bicameralism at the state level. Articles 79 to 122 govern the Union Parliament, while Articles 168 to 212 govern State Legislatures. This essay examines the composition, structural dynamics, and constitutional nuances of India's legislative organs.

Union Legislature: Parliament

Under Article 79, Parliament consists of the President and two Houses: the Rajya Sabha and the Lok Sabha. Though the President is not a sitting member of either House, Article 79 makes him an integral part of Parliament because no bill can become law without presidential assent under Article 111.

The Lok Sabha (Article 81) is the popular chamber. Its members are directly elected by citizens on the basis of adult suffrage. The Constitution caps its maximum strength at 550 elected members. Constituencies are demarcated based on population to ensure political equality. Conversely, the Rajya Sabha (Article 80) is the federal chamber representing states and union territories. It is a permanent body not subject to dissolution, with one-third of its members retiring every two years. It comprises up to 238 representatives of states and union territories and 12 members nominated by the President for their special knowledge or practical experience in literature, science, art, and social service.

State Legislatures

At the state level, Article 168 provides for bicameral or unicameral legislatures. While states like Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, and Maharashtra have bicameral systems comprising a Legislative Assembly (Vidhan Sabha) and a Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad), most states are unicameral. The Vidhan Sabha represents direct democracy at the state level, with its composition governed by Article 170. The Vidhan Parishad, governed by Article 171, is modeled on the Rajya Sabha but holds lesser powers; it is purely a deliberative chamber.

Crucially, Article 169 empowers Parliament to create or abolish a State Legislative Council if the Legislative Assembly passes a resolution to that effect by a special majority (a majority of the total membership of the House and a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting). This asymmetrical federal design allows states to decide their own institutional architecture based on financial viability and political will.

Functional Dynamics and Checks

Both Union and State legislatures function through elaborate procedural rules, maintaining independence through privileges and immunities under Articles 105 and 194. Furthermore, the Tenth Schedule checks floor-crossing through strict anti-defection provisions, ensuring structural stability against opportunistic political realignments.

Conclusion

The composition and structure of Indian legislatures reflect a delicate balance between direct democratic accountability (Lok Sabha and Vidhan Sabha) and federal/deliberative checks (Rajya Sabha and Vidhan Parishad). Through constitutional mechanisms like Article 169 and strict delimitation norms, the legislature remains responsive to India's vast socio-political diversity while upholding the supremacy of the Constitution.
2.exam_angle: Examiners frequently test this topic through both 5-mark short notes (e.g., 'Abolition of Legislative Councils under Article 169') and 15-mark essays ('Compare and contrast the composition and powers of Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha'). To score high, do not merely list numbers of seats; discuss the federal significance of the Rajya Sabha and the unique mechanism of Article 169 with case law backing.
quick_recap: Union Parliament = President + Rajya Sabha + Lok Sabha (Article 79).
Rajya Sabha is permanent; Lok Sabha has a 5-year normal term.
State Legislatures can be unicameral or bicameral (Article 168).
Article 169 allows Parliament to create or abolish State Legislative Councils.
Anti-defection rules under the Tenth Schedule safeguard legislative stability.
2.importance_reason: This topic forms the foundational architecture of Unit I and is a staple for both essay and short-note questions in Constitutional Law II examinations.

3.topic: Legislative Powers and Functions of Parliament and State Legislatures
3.lecture_title: Legislative Powers and Functions of Parliament and State Legislatures: The Federal Tug-of-War
3.memory_hook: Think of the Constitution as a strict apartment building code: the Union Parliament legislates for the entire sky-scraper under the Union List, State Legislatures decorate their individual apartments under the State List, and both can paint the hallway together under the Concurrent List, but if a state color clashes with the Union color, the Union paint instantly covers it up.
3.concept_explanation:
India is a federal country with a strong unitary bias, a design choice brilliantly described by Professor K.C. Wheare as 'quasi-federal.' When we examine the legislative powers and functions of Parliament and the State Legislatures under Part XI of the Constitution of India (specifically Articles 245 to 255), we are looking at the fundamental machinery that divides sovereign law-making authority. Territorial jurisdiction is the first baseline: Article 245 establishes that Parliament may make laws for the whole or any part of the territory of India, while a State Legislature may make laws for the whole or any part of the state. Crucially, Parliament possesses the unique power to enact extra-territorial legislation—laws that apply to acts happening outside India but having an impact within it—which state legislatures cannot do.

To manage this massive division of power without constant warfare, the framers adopted the Seventh Schedule, which divides all conceivable legislative subjects into three distinct lists. List I (Union List) contains subjects of national importance like defense, foreign affairs, and railways, where Parliament has exclusive power. List II (State List) contains subjects of local importance like public order, police, public health, and agriculture, where State Legislatures hold exclusive domain. List III (Concurrent List) houses subjects like criminal law, economic and social planning, and education, where both Parliament and States can legislate.

What happens when a state law conflicts with a central law on a Concurrent subject? Article 254 provides the golden rule of resolution: the doctrine of repugnancy. If a state law on a Concurrent List subject is inconsistent with a parliamentary law (whether passed before or after), the parliamentary law prevails, and the state law becomes void to the extent of the repugnancy. However, there is a vital safety valve: if the state law has received the President's assent under Article 254(2), it can prevail within that state, even if inconsistent with an earlier central law, though Parliament can still override it later by passing a fresh law.

Finally, what happens when a subject does not fit neatly into any list? Enter the residuary powers under Article 248 and Entry 97 of the Union List. Unlike the United States or Australia where residuary powers go to the states, in India, residuary powers—powers to legislate on any matter not enumerated in List II or List III—vest exclusively in the Parliament. This structural tilt ensures that whenever a brand-new technological or social phenomenon emerges that the framers could not foresee (such as cyber law or space exploration), the national legislature retains the undisputed authority to act.
key_provisions: Article 245 — Extent of laws made by Parliament and by the Legislatures of States
Article 246 — Subject-matter of laws made by Parliament and by the Legislatures of States (Seventh Schedule Lists)
Article 249 — Power of Parliament to legislate with respect to a matter in the State List in the national interest
Article 254 — Inconsistency between laws made by Parliament and laws made by the Legislatures of States

case_laws.case_name: State of West Bengal v. Union of India
case_laws.facts: The Parliament enacted the Coal Bearing Areas (Acquisition and Development) Act, 1957, empowering the Centre to acquire land and coal mines vested in the State of West Bengal. West Bengal filed an original suit challenging the constitutional validity of the Act, arguing that India is a federal state and Parliament lacked the competence to acquire state-owned property.
case_laws.holding: The Supreme Court held that the Indian Constitution does not establish a traditional federal system akin to the US. It vests supreme power in the Centre, and the states are not sovereign entities possessing co-ordinate authority; thus, Parliament had full competence to enact the law.
case_laws.why_it_matters: It cemented the foundational principle of Indian constitutional law that federalism here is functional, not absolute, and tilt heavily in favor of parliamentary supremacy.

case_laws.case_name: M. Karunanidhi v. Union of India
case_laws.facts: The State of Tamil Nadu enacted the Tamil Nadu Public Men (Criminal Misconduct) Act, 1973, creating offenses relating to corruption by public figures. Later, Parliament enacted the Prevention of Corruption Act and the Code of Criminal Procedure Amendment Act, covering similar ground, prompting a challenge that the state law was void for repugnancy under Article 254.
case_laws.holding: The Supreme Court laid down clear tests for repugnancy: (1) Direct inconsistency between the two laws, (2) Parliament's intent to occupy the entire field, and (3) The state law must have received Presidential assent to save it from earlier central laws if a direct conflict exists. The Court found no irreconcilable direct conflict here, but outlined the doctrine clearly.
case_laws.why_it_matters: This case remains the definitive modern authority on how courts interpret and apply the doctrine of repugnancy under Article 254.

case_laws.case_name: Hoechst Pharmaceuticals Ltd. v. State of Bihar
case_laws.facts: Pharmaceutical companies challenged the validity of a Bihar taxation statute that levied a surcharge on certain sales under the state's taxing power, claiming it interfered with pricing regulations set under central pharmaceutical control legislation.
case_laws.holding: The Supreme Court held that merely because a state law touches upon a subject dealt with by a central law, it does not mean there is repugnancy. The subjects must fall within the same entry and there must be an irreconcilable direct clash.
case_laws.why_it_matters: It establishes that incidental encroachment by state legislatures into fields related to central laws will not automatically void the state enactment.

3.real_world_example: When the Parliament enacted the three controversial Farm Acts in 2020, intense political friction arose because 'Agriculture' is listed as Entry 14 in List II (State List) of the Seventh Schedule. Several state assemblies passed counter-resolutions and attempted to pass their own state-level amendments to nullify the central laws. This modern standoff exemplifies the real-world tension of legislative competence: states argued the Centre was encroaching on their exclusive domain, while the Centre relied on aspects of trade, commerce, and concurrent entries to justify its authority.
3.illustration: Suppose the Parliament enacts a law setting a uniform nationwide speed limit of 100 km/h on all highways under the Concurrent List entry for 'Criminal Law or Transport'. Subsequently, the State Legislature of Telangana passes a law stating that inside reserve forest zones within Telangana, the speed limit must not exceed 40 km/h, and fails to get Presidential assent. Under Article 254, the state law is directly inconsistent with the central rule on speed limits. Therefore, the state law is void to the extent of inconsistency, and the central 100 km/h limit applies, unless the state law can be narrowly construed as a special rule for 'forest protection' under the State List entry for forests, escaping direct repugnancy.
3.quick_answer: The legislative powers of Parliament and State Legislatures are structured by Part XI and the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution. Article 245 defines territorial limits, while Article 246 distributes subjects across three lists: Union List (List I), State List (List II), and Concurrent List (List III). Parliament has exclusive domain over List I, States over List II, and both share List III. Residuary powers belong exclusively to Parliament under Article 248. When a conflict arises between a state law and a parliamentary law on a Concurrent subject, Article 254 applies the doctrine of repugnancy: the central law prevails, rendering the state law void unless saved by obtaining the prior assent of the President under Article 254(2).
3.essay_answer:
Introduction
The distribution of legislative powers is the bedrock of India's constitutional framework. While adopting a federal structure, the makers of the Constitution were acutely aware of the need for a strong central authority to maintain national integrity and economic unity. Consequently, they devised a system of legislative powers under Part XI (Articles 245-255) and the Seventh Schedule that combines federal division with a distinct unitary bias. Understanding how Parliament and State Legislatures derive, execute, and reconcile their law-making powers is essential to comprehending Indian constitutional dynamics.

Territorial and Scheme of Distribution
Article 245 sets the spatial boundaries: Parliament can legislate for the whole or any part of India, possessing extra-territorial competence, while state legislatures are restricted to their respective state territories. The substantive division of subjects is codified in the Seventh Schedule via Article 246. List I (Union List) comprises matters of national interest such as defense, atomic energy, and foreign affairs, reserved exclusively for Parliament. List II (State List) encompasses local matters like police, public order, sanitation, and agriculture, assigned to State Legislatures. List III (Concurrent List) covers areas requiring uniform national policy combined with local implementation, such as criminal law, civil procedure, and economic planning.

Residuary Powers and Overriding Authority
Unlike the United States where unallocated powers revert to the states, Article 248 grants residuary powers—matters not covered in any of the three lists—exclusively to Parliament, reinforced by Entry 97 of List I. Furthermore, the Constitution provides mechanisms for Parliament to invade the State List when national interest demands. Under Article 249, if the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution supported by a two-thirds majority stating that it is necessary in the national interest for Parliament to make laws on a State List matter, Parliament can do so temporarily. Similar extraordinary incursions are permitted during National Emergencies (Article 250) or by consent of states (Article 252).

Doctrine of Repugnancy and Conflict Resolution
Where both Parliament and State Legislatures enjoy concurrent competence under List III, overlaps are inevitable. Article 254 governs such conflicts through the doctrine of repugnancy. As elucidated by the Supreme Court in cases like M. Karunanidhi v. Union of India, if a state law conflicts directly with an existing parliamentary law, the parliamentary law prevails and the state law becomes void to the extent of the repugnancy. However, Article 254(2) provides an escape hatch: if a state law on a Concurrent subject is reserved for the consideration of the President and receives presidential assent, it can prevail in that state despite repugnancy. Even then, Parliament retains ultimate sovereignty and can override or repeal that state law by enacting subsequent legislation.

Conclusion
The legislative scheme in India is a masterclass in dynamic federalism. While states enjoy guaranteed legislative spheres within the State List, the overarching supremacy of Parliament—manifested through residuary powers, emergency provisions, and the doctrine of repugnancy—ensures that centrifugal forces do not fracture national unity. The judicial interpretation of these provisions continues to maintain a delicate, working balance between regional autonomy and national integration.
3.exam_angle: This topic is a massive favorite for long essay questions (10-15 marks) and frequently appears as a problem-based question testing the Doctrine of Repugnancy under Article 254 or Parliament's ability to legislate on State List subjects. To score top marks, do not merely list the articles; cite the Seventh Schedule lists precisely, explain the nuances of M. Karunanidhi tests for repugnancy, and explicitly weave in the 'quasi-federal' character of the Indian Constitution.
quick_recap: Part XI (Articles 245-255) governs the legislative relations between the Union and States.
Seventh Schedule has three lists: Union (List I), State (List II), and Concurrent (List III).
Parliament has exclusive domain over List I and residuary powers (Article 248).
States have exclusive domain over List II, subject to parliamentary override via Articles 249, 250, and 252.
Article 254 (Doctrine of Repugnancy): Central law prevails over conflicting State law on Concurrent subjects unless Presidential assent is obtained.
3.importance_reason: This is a core structural pillar of Constitutional Law II; it forms the foundation for evaluating the validity of any legislation enacted in India and regularly features in both essay and problem-based exam questions.
